analysis.one_liner: Blocks lawsuits against employers over workplace COVID-19 infections, while letting workers who quit over safety collect unemployment.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would shield employers from most lawsuits over workers contracting COVID-19 on the job, was introduced by one House Republican with no cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred workers from suing their employer in state or federal court for injuries caused by catching COVID-19 at work, unless the employer broke a workplace safety law [S3]. In exchange, it would have let a worker who quit because their employer did not address their health concerns still qualify for unemployment benefits [S3]. The bill was referred to three committees in May 2020 and never moved again before the Congress ended [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, and the insurers who cover their liability exposure, gain the most: a worker who catches COVID-19 at work could no longer sue in court unless the employer violated a state or federal workplace safety law [S3]. During a pandemic when it was often impossible to prove exactly where an infection happened, that exception would be hard to use. A smaller group of workers also benefits: someone who quits because the employer did not respond to their health concerns could keep unemployment eligibility by having the quit count as 'through no fault of their own' [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Employers would be exempt from liability in any state or federal court case for injuries resulting from an employee contracting COVID-19 [S3].
The exemption would not apply if the employer violated state or federal law related to workplace safety, leaving workers with a claim only in that narrower case [S3].

A worker who told their employer about health concerns and was unsatisfied with the response (protective equipment, workplace adjustments, or alternative work) could quit and still qualify for state and federal unemployment benefits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who caught COVID-19 on the job would bear the cost: they would lose the ability to recover damages for lost wages, medical costs, or a family member's death, except where the employer violated workplace safety law [S3]. Because infections are hard to trace to a specific workplace, most injured workers would be left with no remedy. State unemployment insurance funds would also absorb the cost of benefit claims from workers who quit over health concerns [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers sickened on the job and state UI funds

drawbacks.text: The bill removes a worker's day in court for the most likely scenarios: during a community-spread pandemic, an employer could argue an infection came from anywhere, making the safety-law exception hard to satisfy and leaving most sickened workers with no compensation [S3].

The bill imposes no new safety requirement on employers before granting the shield; protection for workers rests entirely on the worker first raising a concern and the employer's optional response of equipment, adjustments, or reassignment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is lopsided. Employers get a near-total shield from COVID-19 lawsuits, while workers get a smaller unemployment rule and a liability exception that is difficult to use when infections cannot be traced to a single workplace. The bill also creates no affirmative duty on employers to make workplaces safe before taking away workers' right to sue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees in May 2020 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Turner introduced the bill on May 12, 2020 [S1].
It was referred to the House Judiciary, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees the same day [S5].
No further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers are better off because the bill died: they kept the ability to sue employers over workplace COVID-19 infections, a remedy the bill would have eliminated in all but safety-law-violation cases. Employers are worse off for not gaining the liability shield.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who kept the right to sue

for.name: Michael R. Turner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured no cosponsors; it went no further than committee referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Employers facing COVID-19 lawsuits (retail, food service, manufacturing, health care)
industries.note: Had it passed, these employers would have been shielded from lawsuits by employees who caught COVID-19 at work unless they violated workplace safety law, shifting the cost of illness onto workers and taxpayers. Because the bill died, they keep their current liability exposure.
The bill would have capped insurers' payouts on workplace COVID-19 claims while also removing a basis for employers to demand lower premiums. It died, so nothing changed.
The bill's quit provision would have added benefit claims from workers leaving unsafe jobs, but without workplace protections those costs were already falling on workers. No change resulted.
